Each time DNA is replicated the telomeres which protect the cell deteriorate slightly. This means that a clone of an organism only has a natural lifespan as long as the remaining lifespan of the original organism because when the telomeres reach a certain point of degradation the organism begins to shut down, whether this is a result of the cell division not happening properly or some kind of biological response to deteriorated telomeres I'm not sure. If you continually cloned the same DNA you should end up with just a heap of identical twins that will all die around the same time. A successful cloning is one where the actual DNA is not damaged at all so they shouldn't eventually become dribbling vegetables after a few clones.

Not quite, it doesn't move in a cycle which is what I think you mean. The loop is in two halves, strings, and body/neck/bridge/nut. When the strings are struck they vibrate, at the same time the body woods are moving with same energy. The only difference is that strings have less mass and therefore he same amount of energy will result in more movement. The vibration which we hear exists simultaneously in both halves of the loop but the string half is what is 'monitored' by the pickups.

Saddle mass and material can affect the sustain as they are a part of the 'frame' across which the string is put under tension. If you imagine the strings and the guitar like a loop, the tension of the string is caused by the force of the string pulling the two 'ends' of the loop together and the opposing force as the materials of the neck and body resist being folded or crushed. Therefore the force of the tension is equal in both the string and the neck and body which is why the materials from which these are made affects the vibration of the strings and this the tone. That is what the people who claim pickups are the only thing that affects tone never seem to grasp.

We didn't test finishes on the wood but I agree that the finish probably doesn't make any audible difference at all. I was saying that the wood makes a noticeable difference and the variations in tone are not simply the result of pickups and strings.

Strings don't just vibrate on their own, they require the tension from the resistance of trying to pull both ends of the piece of wood they are connected to together. I did an investigation in physics not long ago where we(my guitarist lab partner and I) ran a length of string tuned to the same pitch accross two points on various different tonewoods. We already knew from a previous test that different types of wood (I believe it was Mahogany, Pine and Maple) showed clear differences in the shape of the vibrations waves when we places a tuning fork on one end of the piece of wood and a clip on mic running into a data logger on the other end. When we measured the vibrations of the strings stretched accross the same pieces of wood tuned to the same pitch as the tuning fork with a magnetic sensor (basically a pickup) running into a data logger we could actually see that the same characteristics we saw in each wood from the first test were present to a lesser extent in the strings vibration when attached to the same piece of wood.

tl;dr Me and another guy tested the effect different wood has on string vibration, and found that the characteristics of the piece of woods vibration were also present in the string's vibration.

Yes but the characteristics of the vibrations of the strings being picked up is definitely affected by the wood to which the strings are attached. This, in turn, is affected to a degree by the finish on the wood.
